notes.title: How the cuisine filters were policed
notes.body: Every food card names a specific dish — a cuisine label alone doesn’t qualify. The region’s signature strengths are the half-smoke (Ben’s Chili Bowl), DC’s Ethiopian corridor along U Street, the area’s Salvadoran pupuserias, Chesapeake blue crab and oysters, the jumbo slice, and the Vietnamese sprawl of Eden Center — alongside a deep Michelin and James Beard fine-dining bench. A cuisine tag names the kitchen’s own tradition, never one dish it happens to serve.

notes.title: Web-searched, merit-measured and fact-checked
notes.body: Every place is traceable to a credible source — Michelin, James Beard, Washingtonian, the Washington Post, Eater DC, Northern Virginia Magazine, ARLnow, the National Park Service and the Smithsonian — recorded in data/sources.json (direct map/page fetches are blocked in the build environment, so sources were confirmed via search). A mention is not merit: each place is measured for acclaim (award, rave, or a high rating with real volume) before it earns a pin. Every coordinate is verified into data/geocodes.json and every place status-checked open.

places.ad: 2 Lincoln Memorial Cir NW, Washington, DC 20037
places.w: Henry Bacon's Doric temple (1922) housing Daniel Chester French's 19-foot seated Lincoln, the terminus of the Reflecting Pool and the spot where Dr. King delivered 'I Have a Dream.' Open 24 hours, free, ranger-staffed.

The 555-foot marble obelisk (completed 1884) honoring the first president, the tallest structure in DC. Grounds are open daily; the interior elevator to the observation deck has faced repeated closures, so check NPS for current top access before you go.

places.ad: 16 E Basin Dr SW, Washington, DC 20242
places.w: John Russell Pope's domed rotunda (1943) on the Tidal Basin, with a 19-foot bronze of Jefferson ringed by his own words. One of the finest cherry-blossom vantage points each spring.

A plaza of 56 granite pillars and two arches around a fountain between the Washington Monument and the Reflecting Pool, dedicated 2004 to the 16 million who served. The Freedom Wall bears 4,048 gold stars.

places.ad: 5 Henry Bacon Dr NW, Washington, DC 20037
places.w: Maya Lin's stark black-granite wall (1982) inscribed with the 58,000-plus names of the fallen and missing, sunk into the earth beside the Three Soldiers statue. Among the most-visited and most-moving sites on the Mall.

places.ad: 10 Daniel French Dr SW, Washington, DC 20024
places.w: Nineteen stainless-steel soldiers advance through juniper toward an American flag, mirrored on a granite wall to read as 38 (the 38th parallel). The 2022 Wall of Remembrance added the names of the dead.
A 30-foot 'Stone of Hope' likeness of Dr. King emerging from a split boulder on the Tidal Basin's northwest rim, opened 2011. A 450-foot inscription wall carries 14 of his quotations.

places.ad: 1850 West Basin Dr SW, Washington, DC 20242
places.w: A 7.5-acre sequence of four granite outdoor 'rooms,' one per FDR term, threaded with waterfalls, sculpture and quotations. Opened 1997 on the Tidal Basin's Cherry Tree Walk.

The man-made inlet ringed by the Jefferson, FDR and MLK memorials and by 3,000-plus Yoshino cherry trees, a 1912 gift from Tokyo that draws peak-bloom crowds each late March. Paddleboats and a walking loop year-round.

The Smithsonian's flagship of flight and spaceflight, home to the Wright Flyer, Spirit of St. Louis, and Apollo 11 command module. Reopened in full for its 50th anniversary in July 2026 after a multi-year renovation; free, timed passes recommended.

places.ad: 10th St & Constitution Ave NW, Washington, DC 20560
places.w: The Smithsonian's natural-history giant, home to the Hope Diamond, a live butterfly pavilion, dinosaurs and the Ocean Hall. Free admission, one of the most-visited museums on earth.
Keeper of the original Star-Spangled Banner, the Ruby Slippers, Julia Child's kitchen and the First Ladies' gowns. A free Smithsonian survey of the American story.

places.n: National Museum of African American History and Culture
places.w: David Adjaye's bronze-corona building (opened 2016), the Smithsonian's newest and among its most sought-after, tracing slavery through the present across culture, sport and struggle. Free, but timed passes are advised.

places.ad: Independence Ave SW & 7th St SW, Washington, DC 20560
places.w: The Smithsonian's modern and contemporary art museum, a cylindrical 'donut' by Gordon Bunshaft with a sunken sculpture garden across Jefferson Drive. Free; strong in Rothko, Bourgeois and immersive installations.

places.ad: 6th St & Constitution Ave NW, Washington, DC 20565
places.w: The nation's art museum (not a Smithsonian), pairing John Russell Pope's neoclassical West Building with I.M. Pei's East Building, plus a sculpture garden. Free; home to the only Leonardo da Vinci in the Americas.

A living plant museum at the foot of Capitol Hill, its 1933 glass Conservatory holding a jungle, orchids and a seasonal garden-railway show. Free, and one of the oldest continually operating botanic gardens in the country.

The executive mansion and workplace of every president since John Adams, viewable from Lafayette Square and the south Ellipse. Interior tours are free but must be arranged well ahead through a member of Congress.
Home of the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution and the Bill of Rights, displayed in the Rotunda for the Charters of Freedom. Free admission.

places.n: Smithsonian American Art Museum & National Portrait Gallery
places.w: Two free Smithsonian museums sharing the Greek Revival Old Patent Office Building in Penn Quarter, joined by the glass-roofed Kogod Courtyard. The Portrait Gallery's 'America's Presidents' is the only complete set outside the White House.
The still-operating 1863 theater where Lincoln was shot on April 14, 1865, now an NPS site with a museum and the Petersen House (where he died) across the street. Working stage plus historical tours.

A soaring 1887 Great Hall lined with 75-foot Corinthian columns, once the Pension Bureau, now devoted to architecture, design and engineering. Known for blockbuster summer installations; the Great Hall is free.
A privately run, glass-clad museum of espionage at L'Enfant Plaza, with one of the largest public collections of spy artifacts and interactive tradecraft exhibits. Ticketed admission.
A 75-foot, seven-roof gate over H Street (1986), the largest single-span Chinese archway of its kind, marking the entrance to DC's compact Chinatown near Capital One Arena.

places.n: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts
places.w: The nation's living memorial to JFK and its busiest performing-arts complex, on the Potomac beside the Watergate, home to the National Symphony and Washington National Opera. Free daily performances on the Millennium Stage and a rooftop terrace with river views.

The cobblestoned C&O Canal towpath and the Potomac-front park frame Georgetown's shops and rowing crews, with mule-drawn boat history at the NPS canal. A walkable stretch of the neighborhood's 18th-century core.

A Harvard-run research estate in upper Georgetown celebrated for its Byzantine and Pre-Columbian art and, above all, Beatrix Farrand's terraced formal gardens. Museum is free; the gardens are ticketed in season.
Built in 1765, the oldest unchanged building in DC and a rare survivor of pre-Revolutionary Georgetown, now an NPS house museum with a colonial-style garden. Free.

The oldest Catholic and Jesuit university in the United States (founded 1789), whose Flemish-Romanesque Healy Hall and its clock-tower spires crown the campus above the Potomac. Grounds are open to visitors.

America's first museum of modern art (1921), an intimate Dupont Circle mansion whose crown jewel is Renoir's 'Luncheon of the Boating Party,' plus a meditative Rothko Room. Ticketed for special exhibitions.

The Massachusetts Avenue stretch northwest of Dupont Circle lined with more than 50 embassies and Gilded Age mansions, marked by statues of Gandhi, Churchill and Mandela. A self-guided architectural walk.

places.ad: 18th St NW & Columbia Rd NW, Washington, DC 20009
places.w: DC's most eclectic nightlife-and-dining strip, famous for its murals, international restaurants and the late-night jumbo slice. A lively, walkable neighborhood core.

The traffic-circle park at the heart of the neighborhood, its 1921 marble fountain designed by the Lincoln Memorial's team, ringed by bookstores, cafes and a Sunday farmers market. A classic people-watching green.

places.n: African American Civil War Memorial & Museum
places.w: A bronze 'Spirit of Freedom' sculpture and a wall inscribed with the 209,000-plus names of the U.S. Colored Troops, paired with a museum around the corner on U Street. Anchors the historic Black cultural heart of the city.

A restored 1922 movie-and-vaudeville palace on 'Black Broadway,' where Duke Ellington, Ella Fitzgerald and Cab Calloway played, now a concert and event venue. A cornerstone of the U Street corridor's revival.
An Italianate terraced NPS park with the longest cascading fountain in North America and, on Sundays, a decades-old drum circle. Known locally as Malcolm X Park.

The seat of Congress crowned by Thomas U. Walter's cast-iron dome and the Statue of Freedom, with the frescoed Rotunda and Brumidi corridors within. Free tours start from the underground Capitol Visitor Center; passes recommended.

The largest library in the world, whose 1897 Thomas Jefferson Building is a Gilded Age showpiece of marble, mosaic and the domed Main Reading Room. Free; home to a Gutenberg Bible and Jefferson's library.

places.n: Supreme Court of the United States
places.w: Cass Gilbert's 1935 marble temple facing the Capitol, its pediment reading 'Equal Justice Under Law.' Free to enter when the court is not in session; visitors can hear argument or view the courtroom.

DC's last of the great 19th-century public markets (1873), still selling produce, meat and crafts inside Adolf Cluss's South Hall, with a weekend flea market and farmers' line outside. The social heart of Capitol Hill.

A mile-long redeveloped Southwest Waterfront of restaurants, live-music halls and piers on the Washington Channel, anchored by the nation's oldest continuously operating fish market. Waterfront promenade, water taxis and boat rentals.
A restored NoMa warehouse turned buzzy food hall with 40-plus local vendors, a rooftop, and a fast-growing district of restaurants and murals around it. Open year-round.
A revived nightlife-and-arts strip northeast of Union Station, centered on the restored Atlas Performing Arts Center and a dense run of bars, small plates and live music. Served by the DC Streetcar.
A design-forward riverfront park on the Anacostia in Navy Yard, with a wave-arched bridge, boardwalk and canal basin beside Nationals Park. Free summer concerts and fountains for kids.

The nation's most hallowed military cemetery, 639 acres of some 400,000 graves, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier with its round-the-clock changing of the guard, and President Kennedy's eternal flame. Free; open daily.

places.n: U.S. Marine Corps War Memorial (Iwo Jima)
places.w: Felix de Weldon's 32-foot bronze of the flag-raising on Mount Suribachi, dedicated 1954 just north of Arlington Cemetery. An NPS site with sweeping views back to the Mall.

places.ad: 1 Air Force Memorial Dr, Arlington, VA 22204
places.w: Three stainless-steel spires arcing 270 feet skyward in the 'bomb burst' of the Thunderbirds, on a ridge overlooking the Pentagon and the city. Free, open daily; striking at sunset.

places.ad: George Washington Memorial Pkwy, Arlington, VA 22202
places.w: A riverside NPS lawn at the north end of Reagan National's main runway, where jets roar overhead just above your head on final approach. Free plane-spotting, picnicking and Mount Vernon Trail access.

places.ad: George Washington Memorial Pkwy, Arlington, VA 22209
places.w: An 88-acre wooded Potomac island preserved as a living memorial to the conservationist president, laced with swampy trails and centered on a 17-foot bronze of TR. Reached by footbridge from a GW Parkway lot; free.

A mile of preserved 18th- and 19th-century streets running from the King Street Metro down to the Potomac, packed with independent shops, taverns and George Washington history. A free trolley links the waterfront to the top of the hill.

places.ad: 3200 Mount Vernon Memorial Hwy, Mount Vernon, VA 22121
places.w: Washington's meticulously restored Potomac plantation home, 16 miles south of the city, with the mansion, his tomb, working farm, and museums on his life and the people he enslaved. Ticketed; a full half-day day trip.
A WWII munitions plant on the Alexandria waterfront reborn as a warren of 80-plus working artist studios and galleries you can walk through. Free admission.
A restored 1785 tavern and 1792 hotel where Washington, Jefferson and Adams dined and danced, now a city museum with a still-operating period restaurant next door. Ticketed tours.
The revitalized Potomac edge at the foot of King Street, with promenade, public art, boat tours and water-taxi service to The Wharf and National Harbor. Free to stroll.

An 800-acre NPS park in McLean where the Potomac crashes through the jagged Mather Gorge in a series of dramatic falls, with three clifftop overlooks and hiking beside the 18th-century Patowmack Canal. Entrance fee; a short drive from Tysons.

places.n: Wolf Trap National Park for the Performing Arts
places.w: The only U.S. national park dedicated to the performing arts, whose open-air Filene Center seats 7,000 for a summer season of pop, classical and dance on 117 wooded acres. Lawn tickets and picnics are the local ritual.
A 95-acre NOVA Parks garden in Vienna with lakes, native-plant and Korean bell gardens, an atrium conservatory, and the popular winter Walk of Lights. Ticketed; peaceful and stroller-friendly.

places.ad: 14390 Air and Space Museum Pkwy, Chantilly, VA 20151
places.w: The Smithsonian Air and Space Museum's cavernous companion by Dulles, hangaring the Space Shuttle Discovery, a Concorde, the SR-71 Blackbird and the Enola Gay. Free admission (paid parking); an aviation day out in the Dulles corridor.

Reston's walkable, European-style downtown of shops, restaurants, a cinema and a central pavilion that becomes an ice rink in winter. The social hub of the Dulles Toll Road suburbs, on the Silver Line.

The largest Vietnamese American commercial center on the East Coast, a Falls Church strip of 120-plus shops, groceries, cafes and restaurants marked by a pagoda gate and clock tower. The cultural and culinary heart of NoVA's Vietnamese community.

places.ad: 115 E Fairfax St, Falls Church, VA 22046
places.w: The 1769 colonial-era Episcopal church that gave the city its name, where George Washington served as a vestryman, still an active parish. A National Register landmark.

A mixed-use Merrifield district built around a green, with an arthouse Angelika cinema, chef-driven restaurants, a Saturday farmers market and design shops. A polished NoVA gathering spot just off I-66.

places.n: National Museum of the United States Army
places.w: The Army's national museum on the public side of Fort Belvoir (no ID or pass needed), opened 2020, telling nearly 250 years of soldiers' stories through immersive galleries, real tanks and a rooftop overlook. Free admission and free parking; timed-entry tickets recommended.

A 55-acre arts campus in the repurposed Lorton Reformatory, with a dozen galleries, 65-plus resident artist studios, live theater and music, and the Lucy Burns Museum on the suffragists jailed here. Second-Saturday open houses, Brewfest and a July 4 festival draw crowds; galleries free to browse.

The historic core of the City of Fairfax around Old Town Square and the 1900 Old Town Hall, with boutiques, sidewalk cafes, the Fairfax Museum & Visitor Center in an 1873 schoolhouse, and festivals from Chocolate Lovers to Fall for the Book. Free spring/fall walking tours cover the Civil War-era streets.

The 1794 home of Richard Bland Lee, Northern Virginia's first congressman and uncle of Robert E. Lee, preserved by the Fairfax County Park Authority beside Dulles Airport. Guided house tours plus a 'Forgotten Road' walking tour of the original outbuildings and enslaved-workers' quarters; grounds and trails are free.

Reston's original 1960s village center on the National Register of Historic Places, a modernist waterfront plaza founder Robert E. Simon designed and lived above, with a boardwalk, restaurants, a Saturday farmers market and kayak rentals on the lake. The 'Bronze Bob' bench statue honors Simon lakeside.

A 130-acre Fairfax County working 1930s-era farm with 100-plus animals to meet, a restored 1918 Herschell carousel, wagon rides, a country store and nature trails. Free admission and parking (rides carry small fees); a favorite family day out near Herndon.

places.ad: Herndon Depot, 717 Lynn St, Herndon, VA 20170
places.w: A 45-mile paved rail-trail on a former railroad bed, running from Shirlington in Arlington out through Falls Church, Vienna, Reston, Herndon and Leesburg to Purcellville, and used by roughly two million walkers, cyclists and runners a year. The Herndon Depot marks a classic downtown trailhead; managed by NOVA Parks.

Virginia's first fully accessible playground (2006), a two-acre space where children of all abilities play side by side across four themed 'rooms,' with rubberized surfacing, a Liberty wheelchair swing and a ground-level, wheelchair-accessible carousel. Free; a trackless train runs seasonally.

One of the largest shopping malls on the East Coast, open since 1968 with 300-plus stores including Apple, Nordstrom and Bloomingdale's, plus an AMC theater and the 1.5-acre outdoor PenFed Plaza that hosts concerts, holiday light shows and family events. On the Silver Line at Tysons.

A Fairfax County park in Great Falls whose observatory holds three permanent telescopes under a roll-off roof, run with the volunteer Analemma Society for free Friday-night public viewing. In 2026 it earned an International Dark Sky 'Urban Night Sky Place' designation - a rare dark sky this close to DC. Programs require advance registration.

A 36-acre Arlington County park between Crystal City and the 14th Street Bridge, with a three-quarter-mile esplanade delivering monumental Potomac and DC skyline views for walking, birdwatching and plane-spotting, plus a $60M aquatics-and-fitness center with a competition pool, lazy river and slides. Free grounds; center is ticketed.

A Tony Award-winning professional theater (2009 Regional Theatre Tony) in the Village at Shirlington, called a 'musical theater powerhouse' by The Washington Post, staging Broadway-caliber musicals and premieres in two intimate spaces. Winner of 100-plus Helen Hayes Awards and the cultural anchor of Shirlington.

The Drug Enforcement Administration's free museum by Pentagon City, reopened after a two-year renovation with the interactive 'Illegal Drugs in America: A Modern History' exhibit tracing trafficking from the 1850s opium wars to today. Open Tuesday-Saturday; steps from the Pentagon City Metro.

A revitalized mixed-use district on the Orange/Silver Line, centered on the Quarter Market food hall (18 globally-inspired stalls), Punch Bowl Social, and the MedStar Capitals Iceplex where the Washington Capitals practice and the public can skate. A walkable Arlington dining-and-entertainment hub.

The definitive home of DC's signature half-smoke, a U Street institution since 1958. A James Beard Foundation "America's Classics" honoree (2004) and Bon Appetit "Best Chili Spots" pick; the half-smoke — a spicier, coarser pork-and-beef sausage smothered in Ben's chili — is the top seller and a genuine city icon.

Chef Jamie Leeds's Dupont original, repeatedly voted DC's best raw bar and seafood restaurant and praised by Washingtonian, Bon Appetit and Food & Wine. The seafood plateau, Maine-style lobster roll and Chesapeake crab cakes headline a menu built around East Coast oysters.

A New England-leaning Navy Yard raw bar on the Anacostia waterfront, a Washingtonian 100 Very Best pick known for its oyster selection, lobster roll and Nashville-hot soft-shell crab. A reliable Chesapeake-and-Northeast seafood room by the ballpark.

The first Ethiopian restaurant on the H Street Corridor and one of the most polished in the city, recommended by Washingtonian and consistently rated among DC's best Ethiopian tables. Bright combination platters and a strong vegetarian beyaynetu on house injera.

A block from the White House, DC's oldest saloon (1856) runs one of the city's busiest raw bars and its annual Oyster Riot. A tourist-and-lobbyist institution whose oysters on the half shell and crab cakes make it a dependable Chesapeake stop downtown.

Ashok Bajaj's first DC restaurant (1989), a genteel colonial-era dining room a block from the White House long favored by presidents and cabinet secretaries. A Washingtonian mainstay whose refined North Indian cooking helped set the template for the city's upscale Indian scene.

A 24-hour Crystal City Afghan institution famous with cab drivers and late-night crowds for its charcoal-grilled kabobs, fluffy rice and fresh naan. A long-running ARLnow and Washingtonian cheap-eats favorite with heavy, high-rated review volume.

A Columbia Heights hole-in-the-wall — Selena art on the walls, ranchera on the jukebox — turning out plump, well-stuffed pupusas with curtido for a couple dollars each. Repeatedly named among DC's best pupuserias; Salvadorans are the city's largest immigrant group and this is one of the canon rooms.

A rough-and-ready Arlington crab house since 1979 and one of the last true steamed-blue-crab feasts inside the Beltway — Old Bay-dusted Maryland blues by the dozen, hammers and paper on the table. A multi-generational local institution keeping the Chesapeake crab-feast tradition alive in NoVA.

The no-frills, cash-only pho institution of the DC area — communal tables, one thing done superbly: deeply aromatic beef pho ladled in vast bowls. A decades-old Washingtonian and Eater DC benchmark that set the standard for the region's Vietnamese noodle soup.

The Seven Corners/Willston Cantonese landmark that started at Eden Center in the early '80s and has carved tableside Peking duck "with care bordering on reverence" ever since — long rated among the best duck and dim sum in the region. Reviewed by Washingtonian and Northern Virginia Magazine (which singled out the Peking duck, steamed spare ribs and wu gok).

A Falls Church destination for tableside Sichuan hot pot — dunk meats, seafood, tofu and noodles into a fiery Chengdu broth (mild available), open till midnight. Reviewed by the Washington Post and a standing recommendation in Tyler Cowen's Ethnic Dining Guide, which praises its classic ingredient list and fair prices. (Permanently closed 2026 — kept flagged.)

The Eden Center specialist for chả ốc — Huế-style rolls of pork studded with snail for a clam-like snap, in a garlic-rich sauce — a dish you won't easily find elsewhere on the East Coast. Owner Huy Pham brought the Garden Grove, CA original east to the region's Little Saigon.

A take-out Eden Center institution and, per Arlington Magazine, "best of breed" for Vietnamese chả — house pork sausage (chả lụa), fried chả chiên and cinnamon chả quế, plus bánh bao and bánh chưng. A daily-staple counter for the local Vietnamese community.

One Michelin star — chef Chetan Shetty (ex-Indian Accent) reinvents Indian fine dining in a regal Penn Quarter room; the Washington Post calls it adventurous Indian cooking in a regal setting. Starred in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide.
One Michelin star — Fabio Trabocchi's luxe downtown Italian, a longtime power-dining room off Pennsylvania Avenue. Holds its star in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide Washington, D.C.

DC's most acclaimed Indian restaurant — Ashok Bajaj's Penn Quarter icon, whose crackling palak chaat is a citywide signature; a MICHELIN Guide recommended pick and a perennial Washingtonian 100 Very Best.
MICHELIN Bib Gourmand — chef John Manolatos's glam East End Italian, whose viral 40-layer lasagna became a citywide sensation. Named a Bib Gourmand in the MICHELIN Guide Washington, D.C.
Two Michelin stars — Ryan Ratino's intimate upstairs tasting counter on 14th Street, DC's only two-star outside minibar and the Inn at Little Washington. Held both stars in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide.
One Michelin star — Ryan Ratino's honey-themed 14th Street bistro (below Jont), starred every year since it opened. Retains its star in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide Washington, D.C.
One Michelin star — Jeremiah Langhorne's wood-hearth Shaw restaurant championing Mid-Atlantic ingredients; starred every year since the DC guide launched in 2017 and a former Washingtonian #1.
One Michelin star and a Michelin Green Star — Rob Rubba's vegetable-forward Shaw room; Rubba won the James Beard Award for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic (2023). Starred in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide.

One Michelin star — Carlos Delgado's upscale Peruvian in Blagden Alley (with casual Amazonia below); Delgado won the James Beard Award for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic (2025). Starred in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide.
James Beard Award for Best New Restaurant (2018) — a soaring, live-fire Middle Eastern and North African room where everything meets an open wood fire; a Washingtonian 100 Very Best mainstay.

One Michelin star — chef Yuan Tang's four-course, choose-your-own-adventure menu on the 14th Street corridor, drawing from the Carolinas, Thailand, France and Japan. Retains its star in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide.
Stephen Starr's landmark Logan Circle brasserie — the see-and-be-seen French cafe that anchored the 14th Street revival; a Washingtonian 100 Very Best and one of DC's hardest tables.
One Michelin star — chef Enrique Limardo's Mediterranean-meets-Latin-American cooking in the West End, a chef's-table experience of bold, cross-continental plates. Starred in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide.
Fabio Trabocchi's glamorous Georgetown waterfront seafood room on the Potomac at Washington Harbour — a Washingtonian 100 Very Best and the marquee special-occasion table on the water.
One Michelin star — Michael Rafidi's live-fire Palestinian restaurant in The Yards; Rafidi won the James Beard Award for Outstanding Chef (2024). Retains its star in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide.
One Michelin star — Aaron Silverman's beloved Barracks Row room, whose lychee-and-pork-sausage salad made it a national name. Starred in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide Washington, D.C.

One Michelin star — Aaron Silverman's all-inclusive, playful fine-dining tasting menu next to Rose's Luxury on Barracks Row; one of DC's most sought-after reservations. Starred in the 2025 MICHELIN Guide.

James Beard Award-winning chef Kwame Onwuachi's Afro-Caribbean flagship at Salamander DC near the Wharf; Washingtonian's #2 restaurant and a Conde Nast Traveler / Esquire Best New Restaurant. Opened 2024 to national acclaim.

Arlington's standout for Balkan small plates — an all-you-can-eat spread of cevapi, ajvar and sarma that made it a Clarendon fixture and a Washingtonian/regional-award favorite; the strongest fine-casual pick in Arlington.
James Beard Award-winning chef Cathal Armstrong's breezy waterfront room at Hotel Indigo; Washington Post critic Tom Sietsema has called it Old Town's most appealing place to eat.

places.ad: 2941 Fairview Park Dr, Falls Church, VA 22042
places.w: A longtime Northern Virginia fine-dining destination — chef Bertrand Chemel's contemporary American cooking with French and Mediterranean influences, set beside koi ponds and a lakeside view; a Falls Church special-occasion standard-bearer.

The city's benchmark for traditional Japanese dining: a MICHELIN-starred kaiseki-and-sushi room above a Dupont Circle CVS, run by second-generation chef Nobu Yamazaki, who reinvented the family restaurant into an upmarket kaiseki house. The MICHELIN star is a lone institutional authority; Time Out ranks it among DC's very best Japanese. Fish is flown from Toyosu.

Sichuan legend Peter Chang's polished DC flagship, where he applies precision to Sichuan and classic Chinese cooking without dialing down the heat. The Washington Post's Tom Sietsema reviewed it as "worth the wait," Esquire named it a Best New Restaurant (2023), and it carries a MICHELIN Guide listing; The Infatuation is a fan. Peter Chang is a past James Beard finalist.

The restaurant that introduced DC to serious ramen (2013): a Sapporo-style ramen bar downstairs with noodles handcrafted and imported from Japan, and a full izakaya upstairs, from chef Katsuya Fukushima. A perennial Eater essential; The Infatuation and Gayot both rate it a Chinatown/Penn Quarter must, and there's usually a line.

DC's upscale West African flagship (opened 2024) from Nigerian-American founder Ope Amosu, a 175-seat downtown room built around a Nigerian core — egusi, bitterleaf (ofe onugbu), beef suya, Lagos snapper — that shifts to a lounge scene on weekends. Reviewed by The Infatuation and featured in Destination DC's dining coverage; fills a real West African gap for a "Chocolate City."

places.ad: 3155 Mount Pleasant St NW, Washington, DC 20010
places.w: Patrice Cleary's warm Mount Pleasant Filipino restaurant (2015) was named the Washington Post's Restaurant of the Year by Tom Sietsema in 2023 — his highest annual honor. The Southern Foodways Alliance and Positively Filipino have both told its story; a diaspora home-away-from-home for kare-kare, crispy lechon kawali and lumpia.

places.ad: 922 N St NW Rear, Washington, DC 20001
places.w: A playful Hong Kong-style Cantonese spot tucked in Shaw's Blagden Alley with red lanterns and night-market energy — dim sum, cheung fun, chow fun and whole crispy fish. The Washington Post's Tom Sietsema ranked it #7 on his top-10 restaurants; Washingtonian and Time Out both praise it. Real Cantonese cooking inside the District.

Yamrot Ezineh's farm-to-table Ethiopian kitchen in Columbia Heights, spices imported from Ethiopia, standout vegetable dishes (sweet-savory carrot wat, deeply caramelized mushroom tibs) alongside berbere beef and braised-lamb yebeg wat. Named to Washingtonian's 100 Very Best Restaurants (2025) and to the Washington Post's best-Ethiopian roundup (2025).

Chef Prince Matey's home-cooked Ghanaian mainstay in Shaw (2015), which Eater calls "Shaw's essential Ghanaian mainstay" for its stellar groundnut soup, egusi and jollof; Washingtonian folded it into its guide to DC's West African cooking. Live bands on weekends and a diaspora crowd — authentic West African, not a fusion approximation.

places.ad: 2700 New York Ave NE, Washington, DC 20002
places.w: The genuine-article Sichuan and Shaanxi kitchen hidden inside a Days Inn off New York Avenue NE. The Washington Post's $20 Diner said it "dazzles"; Tyler Cowen's Ethnic Dining Guide calls it the best Chinese restaurant DC has ever had, with the best dan dan noodles the area has seen; Washington City Paper chronicled its cult following.

Chef Peter Prime's small, bright H Street ode to Trinidad's Indian-African-Chinese street food — doubles, dhalpuri roti, jerk, oxtail and Caribbean rums. A MICHELIN Bib Gourmand honoree repeatedly (2020, 2024, 2025), a lone institutional authority; even Obama has been photographed eating a double there.

Rasika alums Suresh Sundas and Dante Datta's low-lit "Indian-ish" bar-restaurant off H Street — tandoori lamb chops, black dal moored with burrata, inventive cocktails. In the MICHELIN Guide (2022), on the New York Times' 50 Best New Restaurants in America, and a Washingtonian 100 Very Best pick; The Infatuation is a fan.

Erik Bruner-Yang's genre-bending H Street Taiwanese-Cambodian restaurant, cafe and retail concept — dumplings, noodles and a cult twice-fried chicken. The Washington Post reviewed it as a party you can slurp, sip and shop through; The Infatuation calls the Taiwanese-Cambodian hybrid a standout. A rare Taiwanese anchor inside the District.

Ethiopian dining inside a classic Georgetown townhouse — soothing rooms, attentive service that walks newcomers through the menu, and a much-praised doro wot. A MICHELIN Bib Gourmand honoree (2021 onward), a lone institutional authority, and the rare authentic Ethiopian option west of the Little Ethiopia corridor.

James Beard finalist Peter Chang's Fairfax homage to the women of his family (recipes from his mother and wife Lisa; daughter Lydia Chang runs it) — regional Hubei home cooking alongside his cult Sichuan classics. The Washington Post's Tim Carman reviewed it as a new star "powered by women," it ranked #14 on Washingtonian's 100 Very Best Restaurants (2020) and has stayed a fixture through the 2025 and 2026 lists, The Infatuation calls it "Peter Chang's best effort yet," and it's listed in Tyler Cowen's Ethnic Dining Guide. NoVA food creator @urnovafoodie's viral all-you-can-eat dim-sum reel put its weekday dim sum on the map. Open and reviewed into 2026 (Yelp ~996 reviews, ~4.5).

Arlington's legendary Peruvian charcoal-chicken counter in Virginia Square, a decades-old cult institution whose aroma reaches a block away; a Washingtonian award winner for Best Peruvian Chicken and a Roadfood-anointed classic.

James Beard-nominated chef Matt Hill's family-friendly Southern smokehouse; a 2022 RAMMY winner and voted the No. 1 reader-favorite restaurant in Virginia by Washingtonian, with a Washington Post rave for its barbecue and brunch biscuits.

A chic French New-American bistro in the heart of Clarendon executing comforting classics with classic French technique; reviewed favorably by Northern Virginia Magazine and covered as a Clarendon draw by ARLnow.
The upscale modern-Greek destination of Tysons/Vienna, a repeat Washingtonian 100 Very Best and ranked No. 2 on Northern Virginia Magazine's 2025 list of the 50 Best Restaurants in Northern Virginia.

The Falls Church comfort-food restaurant from Yuan and Carey Tang of Michelin-starred Rooster & Owl; winner of the 2024 RAMMY for New Restaurant of the Year and a Washingtonian 100 Very Best, with a New York Times nod.
The famous Falls Church Peking-duck house since 1978 and a Bush-family favorite (their booth got Secret Service bulletproof glass); its lacquered duck is a Washingtonian-lauded regional institution.

A cash-friendly Annandale outpost of the Taiwanese Tang-family chain, serving authentic Taiwanese and Northern Chinese street snacks; a longtime Washingtonian Cheap Eats pick and a Tyler Cowen ethnic-dining favorite.

A Fairfax City favorite from the beloved Great American Restaurants group since 1978, called 'the very best in Fairfax' by Washingtonian; a perennially packed, no-reservations American seafood-and-steak house.

The Korean-Vietnamese build-your-own-bowl spot a local dubbed 'the Asian Chipotle,' turned a NoVA phenomenon after Keith Lee (~17M TikTok) opened his 2024 DMV tour here and rated the lemongrass chicken bowl 8.5/10 — the shop went from ~100 to nearly 1,000 orders a day. Covered by the Washington Post and WUSA9. Open (Yelp, July 2026, 160+ reviews).

The viral Asian-inspired croissant bakery (cube croissants; the cream-filled 'Supreme'; cherry-blossom, pistachio-rose, ube flavors) that grew from NoVA farmers-markets to a Chantilly storefront and is opening a permanent Mosaic District space. Arlington Magazine's 'Eat This Now' spotlighted the croissants and NoVA food creator Sandie S. (@adorkandherfork, ~52K) reeled it to a wider audience. Open (Yelp, July 2026, 4.5+ across 120+ reviews).
